t: Valid Permutations for DI Sequence — Counting DP with Prefix Sums
o: We must count permutations of $0..n$ that respect the up/down pattern given by string s. A brute force over all $(n+1)!$ permutations is hopeless for n=200, so we need dynamic programming. The key state idea: build the permutation left to right, tracking the last value placed. Because only relative order matters among remaining numbers, we can normalize: after placing some values, the number of ways to continue depends only on how many unused values are smaller than the last placed one. For example, s = "DID": we count permutations like (1,0,3,2) where each adjacent pair follows D (down), I (up), D (down). With n ≤ 200, an $O(n^2)$ or $O(n^3)$ DP over positions × last-value-rank fits easily.
k: Only the rank of the last element among remaining values matters, not the actual values — this enables a compact DP over 'number of smaller available elements'.
A classic symmetry trick: when we place a new last element, we can imagine removing it from the pool and decrementing all larger remaining values by 1, keeping the state space small.
Prefix sums turn the naive O(n^3) transition into O(n^2) overall.

a.n: Approach 1: Naive DP over last-value rank
a.i: Let dp[i][j] = number of ways to fill the first i+1 positions such that the last placed value has exactly j unused values smaller than it. When extending with 'I', the next last element must have more smaller-values than j... actually with the standard normalization: if s[i-1]=='I' the next element's count of smaller remaining values can be anything ≥ j (we conceptually remove the previous element and shift), giving dp[i][j] = sum of dp[i-1][k] for k < j when previous was 'D'-constrained appropriately. Concretely: dp[i][j] = sum_{k=j}^{i-1} dp[i-1][k] if s[i-1]=='D', else sum_{k=0}^{j-1} dp[i-1][k]. This works because inserting a new maximum-relative element preserves relative order counts.
s: Initialize dp[0][j] = 1 for all j in [0, n] (first element can be any relative rank).
For each position i from 1 to n, for each j in [0, i], sum dp[i-1][k] over k according to whether s[i-1] is 'I' or 'D'.
'I': next element is larger, so its smaller-count j exceeds previous k: sum k in [0, j-1].
'D': next element is smaller: sum k in [j, i-1].
Answer is sum of dp[n][j] over all j.
a.t: O(n^3) — three nested loops over i, j, and the inner summation k.

a.i: Each transition is a range sum of the previous row, so maintain running prefix sums while filling row i. This removes the innermost loop entirely, giving clean O(n^2) time. We can also keep just two rows since row i depends only on row i-1.
s: Keep prev[j] initialized to 1 for all j in [0, n].
For each character c of s, compute cur[j]: if c=='I', cur[j] = prefixSum(prev, 0..j-1); if c=='D', cur[j] = prefixSum(prev, j..i-1) where i is the current length.
Compute these range sums on the fly with a rolling accumulator per row.
After processing all characters, answer is the total sum of the last row.
a.t: O(n^2) — two nested loops; the inner summation is replaced by a rolling prefix sum.
a.sp: O(n) — only two rows of the DP are kept.

w: In an interview, start with the naive O(n^3) DP to establish the state definition, then optimize to prefix sums — interviewers love seeing that progression. Common pitfalls: off-by-one errors in the range bounds (for 'I' the valid previous ranks are strictly less than j; for 'D' they are j through i-1), forgetting the modulo at every accumulation step, and miscounting the first row (all entries are 1, not just one). Edge cases: single-character strings like "D" (answer 1) and "I" (answer 1); all-'I' gives exactly 1 (the identity permutation); all-'D' also gives 1. Likely follow-ups: reconstruct an actual valid permutation (greedy using the same DP), or handle very large n where an O(n log n) divide-and-conquer/FFT-based counting would be needed.
